Authors Affiliations * 1 Section of Rehabilitation, Kanazawa University Hospital, 13-1 Takaramachi, Kanazawa, 920-8641, Japan. * 2 Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Graduate School of Medical Sciences, Kanazawa University, 13-1 Takaramachi, Kanazawa, 920-8641, Japan. * 3 Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, Graduate School of Medical Sciences, Kanazawa University, 13-1 Takaramachi, Kanazawa, 920-8641, Japan. nakase1007@yahoo.co.jp. * 4 Department of Rehabilitation Medicine, Kanazawa University Hospital, 13-1 Takaramachi, Kanazawa, 920-8641, Japan. * PMID: 33797602 * DOI: 10.1007/s00402-021-03877-1 Abstract Introduction: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction using hamstring tendons may involve harvesting of the gracilis tendon in addition to the semitendinosus tendon (ST) depending on the size of the ST graft. However, the effect of gracilis harvesting in addition to ST harvesting on muscle strength, such as the hamstring-to-quadriceps (HQ) ratio, remains unclear. Hence, this study aimed to investigate the effect of gracilis harvesting on subsequent knee muscle strength. Materials and methods: Eighty-two patients who underwent ACL reconstruction were included in this retrospective study. They were divided into the following two groups depending on the tendon graft used for ACL reconstruction: the ST group (41 patients) and the semitendinosus tendon/gracilis tendon (STG) group (41 patients). The isokinetic peak torque of the knee extensor and flexor was measured using a BIODEX dynamometer at a velocity of 60°/s and 180°/s, respectively, 3 and 6 months after ACL reconstruction. The groups were compared in terms of the limb symmetry index (LSI) and HQ ratio. Conclusions: Gracilis tendon harvesting may contribute to a decrease in knee flexor strength and HQ ratio with fast contraction. Thus, the need for gracilis tendon harvesting in ACL reconstruction should be carefully considered. Level of evidence: III. node_outputs.N8:
Surgical and mechanical consequences of tendon harvest are substantial because the procedure directly disrupts the muscle-tendon unit and alters the local biomechanical environment, which can reduce the capacity for full restoration. Direct tissue trauma is a primary issue: hamstring tendon harvest removes a functional component of the muscle-tendon system, reducing the muscle’s ability to generate force and store elastic energy during movement [N4-R1]. That trauma also limits mechanical loading on the remaining muscle, because the harvested tendon is no longer able to act as a lever or contribute to tension transmission, which may slow adaptation and recovery [N4-R1].

Harvesting also changes the healing environment by damaging blood supply and tissue architecture. The evidence suggests that hamstring harvest is associated with loss of strength and functional outcomes, which implies that the local healing response is compromised rather than fully preserved [N2-R4]. A separate study on isolated gracilis tendon harvesting found that strength and functional outcomes may be maintained, but this does not contradict the broader conclusion that the procedure introduces a stressful environment for regeneration [N2-R3]. The evidence also notes that disuse muscle atrophy is initially why muscle mass is lost after ACL surgery, which is consistent with the idea that reduced loading and altered mechanics after harvest create a disuse-atrophy cycle [N2-R5]. That cycle may persist because the harvested muscle cannot fully compensate for the lost tendon’s mechanical role.

On adjacent muscle atrophy and strength, the evidence is mixed but not reassuring. One study found that hamstring harvest is associated with reduced knee flexor strength and a lower hamstring-to-quadriceps ratio, especially with fast contraction, suggesting that adjacent hamstring function is not preserved after harvest [N4-F1]. Another review states that strength and functional results are not affected by hamstring harvest in some studies, while other studies challenge these results [N2-R4]. This heterogeneity is important: it means that some patients may recover strength adequately, but others may experience persistent deficits. The broader literature on ACL surgery also shows that quadriceps weakness can arise from atrophy and activation failure, which supports the idea that adjacent muscles are not immune to post-harvest changes [N2-R2].

Overall, tendon harvest creates a mechanical disadvantage for the muscle, disrupts blood supply and healing, and can induce adjacent atrophy and strength loss. ---

## 1) Tendon tissue is structurally and functionally less regenerative than muscle

The most direct reason tendon harvest is difficult to restore is that tendon tissue is inherently less regenerative than muscle. Tendon is avascular, hypocellular, and highly organized in collagen type I, which makes it structurally different from muscle [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-R5]. This structure is important because tendons rely on a precise extracellular matrix (ECM) and tenocyte architecture to transmit force and withstand tension, and their healing process is dominated by scar formation rather than full regeneration [N1-R2][N1-R4]. In contrast, human skeletal muscle can regenerate completely after injury under controlled conditions, although the limits and regulation of hypertrophy remain complex [N5-R4][N5-R2].

That trauma also limits mechanical loading on the remaining muscle, which can slow adaptation and recovery [N4-R1].

Harvesting also changes the healing environment by damaging blood supply and tissue architecture. The four lines of evidence converge on a single conclusion: restoration after tendon harvest is difficult because the injury itself changes the tissue’s regenerative environment, reduces mechanical loading, and induces adjacent atrophy and strength loss, while compensation can preserve function without fully restoring original size. ## Why is it difficult to fully restore the size of the semitendinosus and gracilis muscles after their tendons are harvested for ACL reconstruction?

The difficulty of fully restoring the size of the semitendinosus and gracilis muscles after tendon harvest is not because the muscle itself is immune to recovery, but because the surgical injury fundamentally alters the biomechanical, biological, and neuromuscular environment that supports muscle growth and function. The four branch reports together explain this as a combination of tissue-specific regeneration limits, direct surgical trauma, compensatory reorganization, and variable recovery outcomes.

---

## 1) Tendon tissue is structurally and functionally less regenerative than muscle

The most direct reason tendon harvest is difficult to restore is that tendon tissue is inherently less regenerative than muscle. Tendon is avascular, hypocellular, and highly organized in collagen type I, which makes it structurally different from muscle [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-R5]. This structure is important because tendons rely on a precise extracellular matrix (ECM) and tenocyte architecture to transmit force and withstand tension, and their healing process is dominated by scar formation rather than full regeneration [N1-R2][N1-R4]. In contrast, human skeletal muscle can regenerate completely after injury under controlled conditions, although the limits and regulation of hypertrophy remain complex [N5-R4][N5-R2].

This means the tendon harvest injury does not simply “remove” a muscle; it removes a highly specialized connective tissue that cannot be restored by the same regenerative mechanisms as muscle. Even when the harvested tendon regenerates, the surrounding muscle may not fully recover its original size and strength because the tendon’s structural role and the local healing environment are disrupted [N1-R1][N1-R4][N1-R2].

---

## 2) Direct tissue trauma and loss of mechanical loading reduce recovery potential

Harvesting the semitendinosus or gracilis tendon directly disrupts the muscle-tendon unit and alters the local biomechanical environment. The evidence shows that hamstring tendon harvest removes a functional component of the muscle-tendon system, reducing the muscle’s ability to generate force and store elastic energy during movement [N4-R1]. That trauma also limits mechanical loading on the remaining muscle, which can slow adaptation and recovery [N4-R1].

Harvesting also changes the healing environment by damaging blood supply and tissue architecture. The evidence suggests that hamstring harvest is associated with loss of strength and functional outcomes, implying that the local healing response is compromised rather than fully preserved [N2-R4]. A separate study on isolated gracilis tendon harvesting found that strength and functional outcomes may be maintained, but this does not contradict the broader conclusion that the procedure introduces a stressful environment for regeneration [N2-R3]. The evidence also notes that disuse muscle atrophy is initially why muscle mass is lost after ACL surgery, which supports the idea that reduced loading and altered mechanics after harvest create a disuse-atrophy cycle [N2-R5].

In other words, the muscle does not simply “wait to grow back.” The injury changes the tissue’s mechanical function and healing context, which makes it harder to restore normal size and strength.

---

## 3) Adjacent muscle atrophy and strength loss persist

The evidence shows that adjacent hamstring muscle is not immune to harvest-related changes. One study found that hamstring harvest is associated with reduced knee flexor strength and a lower hamstring-to-quadriceps ratio, especially with fast contraction, suggesting that adjacent hamstring function is not preserved after harvest [N4-F1]. Another review states that strength and functional results are not affected by hamstring harvest in some studies, while other studies challenge these results [N2-R4]. This heterogeneity is important: it means that some patients may recover strength adequately, but others may experience persistent deficits.

The broader ACL literature also supports this by showing that quadriceps weakness can arise from atrophy and activation failure after ACL surgery, which implies that adjacent muscles are not unaffected by the overall postoperative biological and mechanical stress [N2-R2]. So even if the harvested muscle is not the only affected tissue, its harvest can still contribute to adjacent atrophy and strength loss.

---

## 4) The body compensates, but compensation does not restore original size

After tendon harvest, the body responds with neuromuscular reorganization and gait compensation patterns. The evidence shows that patients with ACL reconstruction exhibit altered neuromuscular control, including higher hamstrings activation and lower vastus medialis activation in the injured leg compared to uninjured controls [N3-R2]. This suggests the nervous system is trying to stabilize the knee by increasing hamstring activity, even if the muscle itself is smaller or weaker. Another study found that cocontraction between quadriceps and hamstrings decreases with improved single-leg landing in ACLR patients, indicating a shift toward more efficient neuromuscular control rather than simple muscle overactivity [N3-R3].

The body also redistributes load and preserves function by altering gait mechanics. The biomechanical compensation literature indicates that neuromuscular adaptation can occur across different phases of movement, including initial ground reaction force phases, to address rotational control deficits [N3-R1]. This means that even if hamstring size is reduced, the patient may still walk and move, because the neuromuscular system is shifting force production and timing to the remaining functional tissues. The evidence also highlights that patients with hamstring autograft ACL reconstruction can report decreased hamstrings performance, yet the overall functional adaptation may still be sufficient to allow participation [N3-R4].

However, compensation does not mean the muscle fully restores its original size. The evidence on regeneration and recovery shows that hamstring tendons often regenerate after harvest, but muscle size and strength recovery is not always complete and varies by study [N6-R3]. Some studies report incomplete strength recovery at 2 years post-ACLR, showing that adaptive recovery can occur through neuromuscular compensation, tissue remodeling, or partial regeneration, even when the original tendon is not fully restored [N6-R1]. But other studies also show that gracilis harvesting is associated with decreased knee flexor strength and lower HQ ratio, indicating that some deficits may persist even with compensation [N4-F1].

---

## 5) Specific semitendinosus and gracilis evidence: regeneration is common, but recovery is variable

The specific evidence on semitendinosus and gracilis tendons shows that hamstring tendons often regenerate after harvest. Reported regeneration rates are 79% for semitendinosus and 72% for gracilis over 1 year, and some studies explicitly state that hamstring tendons regenerate after ACL reconstruction [N6-R3][N6-R2]. A later study found that 50% of patients showed complete tendon regeneration at 6 months, while 29.2% had no regeneration, and mean strength recovery did not fully normalize, highlighting the heterogeneity of outcomes [N6-R1]. Another study found that hamstring tendon regeneration occurs less frequently in older patients and in smokers, but absence of regeneration does not necessarily cause loss of function [N6-R4].

How muscle size and strength recover compared with contralateral or normal limbs is mixed. The evidence on isolated gracilis harvesting reports that strength and functional outcomes may be maintained, but the study does not provide direct comparisons with contralateral limbs [N2-R3]. In contrast, the study on gracilis and semitendinosus harvesting found that the STG group had significantly worse knee flexor strength and a lower HQ ratio at 6 months compared to the ST group, indicating that harvesting additional tendons can reduce strength relative to the group without extra harvest [N4-F1]. This suggests that recovery is not uniform: some muscles may recover well, while others may not.

The evidence also notes that strength and functional results are not universally affected by hamstring harvest, but other studies challenge these results, showing variability across patients and measurement methods [N2-R4]. This heterogeneity is important because it means recovery depends on individual factors and the specific graft protocol used.

---

## 6) Why restoration is difficult in practice

The four lines of evidence converge on a single conclusion: restoration after tendon harvest is difficult because the injury itself changes the tissue’s regenerative environment, reduces mechanical loading, and induces adjacent atrophy and strength loss, while compensation can preserve function without fully restoring original size. The tendon is structurally less regenerative than muscle, and scar tissue and ECM remodeling further impair restoration [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R4]. At the same time, the surgical trauma disrupts the muscle’s biomechanical role and healing context [N4-R1][N2-R4], and adjacent muscles can atrophy and weaken [N2-R2][N4-F1].

So, even when the harvested tendon regenerates, the surrounding muscle may not fully recover its original size because the injury has already altered the load-bearing capacity, healing environment, and neuromuscular adaptation pathways [N1-R1][N4-R1][N6-R1]. That explains why, in practice, it is difficult to fully restore the size of the semitendinosus and gracilis muscles after their tendons are harvested for ACL reconstruction.
